## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Udumbarajātaka* (Ja 298) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya. The story opens with the verse incipit *Udumbarā c’ ime pakkā* ("Ripe are these figs") [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework recorded in the text, the Buddha recounted this birth story while residing at Jetavana monastery, occasioned by a certain monk who had established a hermitage at a frontier village (*paccantagāma*) [Fausböll 1879]. In the story's concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the resident small monkey (*khuddamakkato nevāsiko*) and the visiting large black monkey (*kāḷamahāmakkato āgantuko*) represented figures from the present circumstance, whereas the Bodhisatta was the tree devatā (*rukkhadevatā*) who observed and commented upon the encounter [Fausböll 1879].
